## Initial Use of AI-Assisted Tools

The initial draft of this textbook was written by the author. Subsequent revisions and refinements were supported by digital writing tools, including large language models and grammar-support software, such as Grammarly, Gemini, ChatGPT, and various markdown, text and Python linters. These tools were used to assist with organization, revision, and clarity of exposition. All conceptual content, interpretations, examples, and pedagogical decisions remain the responsibility of the author, who reviewed, edited, and verified all material for accuracy and coherence.

## A Note on How This Reference Text Was Updated and Edited (June 2026)

This reference text was developed to support several courses I teach in analytics, artificial intelligence, business decision-making, and related areas. It is not intended to replace lectures, assigned readings, class discussion, technical documentation, or primary sources. Instead, it is meant to serve as a flexible reference: a place where students can review key ideas, revisit examples, clarify terminology, and connect course concepts across different contexts.

The ideas, structure, examples, and instructional goals in this text are mine. However, the process by which the text was written has changed **substantially** over time. Earlier versions were drafted primarily by me, with AI-enabled writing assistants used in familiar ways: checking grammar, improving clarity, suggesting edits, and helping revise explanations. More recent versions have been produced through a different workflow. Much of the drafting, editing, formatting, and revision is now managed with the assistance of AI agents and sub-agents. My role is to direct the work, evaluate the output, revise where needed, and decide what belongs in the final version.

That distinction matters. It would not be accurate to say that every sentence in this text was manually written by me in the traditional sense. Nor would it be accurate to say that the text was generated independently by AI. The work reflects a human-directed process in which I set the intellectual agenda, define the learning goals, select the examples, evaluate the explanations, and make the final editorial decisions. The writing itself is the product of collaboration between human judgment and AI-based computational systems.

This process is not separate from the subject matter of my courses. Across analytics, artificial intelligence, management, strategy, marketing, and decision-making, we are confronting a basic shift in how intellectual work is produced. For much of modern education and professional life, creating an artifact such as this required humans to perform most of the visible labor directly: drafting, revising, organizing, formatting, checking, and refining. Increasingly, humans are moving into a different role. We design workflows, guide computational systems, evaluate outputs, make judgments, and take responsibility for the final artifact.

That shift creates a real authorship tension. The ideas and instructional intent remain human. The language, organization, and intermediate production steps may be substantially shaped by AI systems. This does not make the work meaningless, but it does require honesty about how the work was created. Authorship is becoming less about personally executing every step of production and more about judgment, direction, accountability, and responsibility for the final result.

Because this text was created with substantial AI assistance, readers should approach it with appropriate caution. I have reviewed and vetted the material, but I make no claim that it is free of errors, omissions, hallucinations, outdated information, or misleading interpretations. Students should treat this reference text as a learning aid, not as an unquestionable authority. When precision matters, especially for definitions, technical claims, empirical statements, legal or policy issues, or current examples, students should verify the material against lectures, assigned readings, documentation, primary sources, and their own reasoning.

The purpose of this text is therefore twofold. First, it is a practical resource for learning course material. Second, it is an example of the kind of human-AI collaboration that you will increasingly encounter in academic, organizational, and professional settings. We should not treat AI systems as magical sources of truth. We should also not dismiss them as merely mechanical tools. They extend human capability in some ways, perhaps diminishing it in others, while also introducing new responsibilities. This text was created in that spirit, and in this co-authored messy world.

-Dr. Joel Davis & ChatGPT June 2026

## Welcome

*Foundations of Analytics & AI* is a modular, evolving textbook designed to introduce the core ideas, computational tools, and analytical workflows that underpin modern data-driven decision-making. The text integrates conceptual understanding with hands-on examples. Including:

- Explanations of key concepts  
- Demonstrations and worked Python examples  
- Short conceptual notes to reinforce essential ideas  
- Mini-labs that integrate skills into complete workflows  

The book is structured so readers can progress linearly or for those with some experience, navigate directly to topics of interest.

---

## How This Textbook Is Organized

The material is grouped into **three major parts**: foundational concepts → computational skills → applied machine learning and AI methods.

---

### **Part I — Conceptual Foundations of Analytics & AI**

These chapters develop the core ideas that unify analytics, machine learning, and AI systems. They are *concept-only* and require no coding background.

- [**Chapter 1 — What Is Analytics and AI?**](textbook_src/ch1_foundations_analytics_ai_split.qmd)  
- [**Chapter 2 — AI Systems: Data, Models, and Logic**](textbook_src/ch2_ai_systems_data_models_logic.qmd)  
- [**Chapter 3 — Data Pipelines & Decision Frameworks**](textbook_src/ch3_data_pipelines_decision_frameworks.qmd)

---

### **Part II — Python & Data Foundations**

These chapters introduce programming concepts and data skills used throughout modern analytics and AI practice.  
They combine explanation with practical Python examples.

- [**Chapter 4 — Python Execution Foundations**](textbook_src/ch4_terminal_paths_envs.qmd)  
- [**Chapter 5 — Python Basics: Data, Control, Functions**](textbook_src/ch5_python_foundations_data_control_functions.qmd)  
- [**Chapter 6 — Working with Tabular Data in Pandas**](textbook_src/ch6_working_with_tabular_data_pandas.qmd)  
- [**Chapter 7 — JSON and APIs for Data Access**](textbook_src/ch7_json_apis_data_access.qmd)  
- [**Chapter 8 — Simulation and Synthetic Data**](textbook_src/ch8_simulation_synthetic_data.qmd)  
- [**Chapter 9 — Visualization: From Data to Insight**](textbook_src/ch9_visualization_from_data_to_insight.qmd)


Readers already familiar with Python may skim or skip based on experience.

---


### **Part III — Machine Learning & Applied AI**  
(*Chapters appear as they are completed.*)

Each chapter in this part will integrate:

1. **Conceptual Foundations**  
2. **Python Implementation**  
3. **Interpretation & Diagnostics**  
4. **Mini-Labs**  

Planned topics include:

- Supervised learning  
- Regression and classification  
- Model evaluation and diagnostics  
- Overfitting and the bias–variance tradeoff  
- ML pipelines  
- Unsupervised learning and clustering  
- PCA and dimensionality reduction  
- Neural networks and deep learning  
- Convolutional networks  
- Large Language Models (LLMs)  
- Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)  

As chapters are released, links will appear here.

## Learning Philosophy

This textbook is built around two reinforcing goals:

### **AI Literacy**  
Understanding how analytical and AI systems are structured, why they behave as they do, and how they influence decision-making.

### **Practical Capabilities**  
Developing the ability to implement real analytical workflows using Python, diagnostic tools, and modern data processing libraries.

---

## Accessing Code and Data

All example code and supporting data for the text are provided in organized folders:

- **`code/`** — downloadable Python scripts and examples  
- **`data/`** — datasets used in demonstrations and mini-labs  

Download the full repository or browse files individually.
